entry.title: In opting for Lula, Brazil made a conservative choice to elect a man of the left over one of the far right
entry.content:
The 2026 elections in Brazil played out amid an widespread assumption repeated around the world: that the country was polarized and that would inform the vote.

But the word “polarization” implies symmetry – and symmetry is something that never existed in the contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. On one side, a moderate center-left politician with a center-right running mate, Geraldo Alckmin. On the other, a representative of the radical right and a member of an international movement that critics say threatens democracies around the world.

Flávio is no mere conservative. While he may be courted and supported by the members of the Republican Party in the U.S., his policies put him more in the mold of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany and Portugal’s Enough, a party that advocates the repatriation of immigrants and a ban on Muslim places of worship.

On the day he launched his candidacy, at an event of Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) in São Paulo, Flávio laid out three of the guiding principles of what his administration would look like. First was the so called “Project Darkness”, a crime-fighting plan inspired by by El Salvador’s hard-right President Nayib Bukele. Second was joining the Shield of the Americas, U.S. President Donald Trump’s military and political initiative for the continent. Thirdly, Flávio laid out plans for the “tesouraço” or “big cut” – a slashing of public spending modeled after Argentinian President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” economic policy. Since he didn’t provide any details, it’s unclear whether it would be just as sharp as Milei’s, but it was enough to strike fear into those who depend on social programs to survive.

Milei himself was at the launch event. He arrived singing the song The Panic Show by the Argentine hard rock band La Renga. Flávio accompanied Milei in the song’s refrain: “Yo soy el león, soy el rey y te destrozaré” (“I am the lion, I am the king, and I will tear you apart”) while dancing along with the Argentine president.

It is, I believe, the form, more than the content, that defines the members of the far-right brotherhood that threatens democracies around the world. They are politicians who do not like to negotiate, even though negotiation is the essence of politics. They want to annihilate the “enemy”, as if they were, literally, on a battlefield.

Misplaced ideas

Flávio’s ideas are clearly “misplaced ideas,” to borrow the term coined by Brazilian literary critic, essayist, and professor Roberto Schwarz. It is impossible to implement Nayib Bukele’s crime-fighting plan — which allows for the arrest of any citizen without a formal charge, the right for legal counsel, or habeas corpus — in a democratic country.

On the economy side, in the midst of a debt crisis, Brazil does needs a fiscal adjustment. However, the country’s economic situation bears no resemblance to that of Argentina, a country that has seen its currency collapse and is rolling over dollar denominated debt.

A recent report in the Financial Times portrayed what is known in Brazil as Bolsonarism as a clan similar to the Roy family from the American television series “Succession.” Nothing could be more apt. Flávio is not Flávio. He is merely a generic offshoot of the Bolsonaro brand. During the Brazilian TV Globo election debate held right before the runoff of last Sunday, Oct. 25, he referred to his now jailed father administration as “our government.” If he were elected president, Flávio would have governed under Jair’s supervision and alongside his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro - a former congressman now living in the U.S. to escape a arrest warrant - who serves as the point of contact between Bolsonarism and the radical and far right around the world.

Eduardo is close to former Hungary prime minister Viktor Orbán, Spain’s Santiago Abascal, president of Spanish far-right party Vox, El Salvador’s Bukele, France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, and the most radical wing of the U.S. Republican Party.

Flávio spent the election campaign trying to pretend he wasn’t like his father. He marketed himself as the “moderate Bolsonaro.” But Bolsonarism, in Brazilian politics, is synonymous with extremism. The mask slipped during his final speech. If he were a democrat, he would have conceded the indisputable defeat suffered on Oct. 25. Instead, he refused to concede and vowed to challenge the results.

A conservative choice

But how did Lula defeat Flávio? My hypothesis is that Brazilians made a conservative choice. Lula has already governed the country three times. Voters know what to expect from him. His opponent, on the other hand, is seen widely as the Brazilian member of a radical global right wing movement, and whose leader is in prison for attempting a coup. The images of vandals destroying the buildings that house the federal executive, legislative, and judicial branches of Brazil’s government on 8 Jan. 2023 – an echo of the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol riot in the U.S. – are still vivid in the memory of Brazilians.

Faced with a choice between something they already know and the unpredictability of extremists, Brazilians opted for the conservative vote. Being prudent, they did not want to risk their democracy.

João Gabriel de Lima não presta consultoria, trabalha, possui ações ou recebe financiamento de qualquer empresa ou organização que poderia se beneficiar com a publicação deste artigo e não revelou nenhum vínculo relevante além de seu cargo acadêmico.
entry.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro is no mere conservative, but a representative of the radical right and a member of an international movement that critics say threatens democracies around the world.

author.name: João Gabriel de Lima, Jornalista, doutorando em Política Comparada, Universidade de Lisboa

entry.title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
entry.content:
Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated Novi Sad train station in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.

Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.

At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.

Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.

Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.

Feelings of solidarity were also experienced when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:

They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.

Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”

At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.

What’s next?

The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.

However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government may seek accountability for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the possibility for revenge to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter.

For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat can bring grief, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, Vučić said: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.”

The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has actively avoided developing a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves.

As one focus group participant said:

Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing.

There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership.

But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices.

Work by Gavin Sullivan and Tereza Capelos on this project was co-funded by the European Union (Horizon Europe, PLEDGE: Political of Grievance and Democratic Governance, PN: 101132560). The views and opinions expressed are, however, those of the authors only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union. The European Union cannot be held responsible for them.

The work of Tereza Capelos was co-funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) under the UK Government’s Horizon Europe Funding Guarantee, grant number 10108342.
entry.summary: A record number of voters turned out to end Alexander Vučić’s longstanding dominance of Serbian politics.

author.name: Gavin Brent Sullivan, Professor of Social Psychology, International Psychoanalytic University Berlin
Tereza Capelos, Professor of Political Psychology, Department of Politics and International Relations, University of Southampton

entry.title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
entry.content:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

Only Getúlio Vargas governed longer. He held power for almost two decades through a revolution, dictatorship and democratic election from the 1930–50s, and is widely considered Brazil’s most consequential president.

Third, no runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media, supporting both sides.

Unlike the first round, the second round was not quiet, nor was it decided by television ads. Brazil saw a mass mobilization of voters, and it was ferocious.

The Brazilian left fought an uphill battle against social media platforms, economic elites, and a Supreme Electoral Court whose president was accused of trying to tip the balance to favour Bolsonaro.

Lula has a long record of political miracles, and he has added another one to the list.

An election result that matters beyond Brazil

Lula’s victory matters well beyond Brazil’s borders, also in three ways.

Globally, Brazil remains a bulwark against the rise of the far right. In recent elections across Latin America and Europe, far-right parties and leaders have advanced almost everywhere.

Brazil, the world’s fourth-largest democracy, has now bucked the trend, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.

Regionally, Lula has defied the so-called “incumbent curse”. Over the past decade in Latin America, governing parties have lost election after election, punished by voters for inflation, insecurity and economic stagnation.

Brazil’s economy was in reasonable shape, but its gains were modest and unevenly felt. Everything pointed to a defeat, and Lula beat the odds anyway.

His win is also a check on what critics have called the “Donroe Doctrine”, referring to the Trump administration’s push to bring the Western Hemisphere more firmly into the US sphere of influence through tariffs, threats and political patronage.

Bolsonaro had campaigned as Washington’s preferred partner in South America. Brazil’s voters turned that offer down.

Domestically, the result also shows the power of popular mobilisation on the left. After Lula’s poor first-round showing, Lula’s campaign re-energised demoralised supporters and built a broad coalition of voters, some of whom were voting less for Lula than against what Bolsonaro represents. It also mobilised people who had stayed home in the first round to get out to vote.

The battle is not over

Lula should not mistake survival for vindication. Yes, he corrected course. In three weeks, he acknowledged the mistakes he made over four years in office, especially during a lacklustre first-round campaign. He sharpened his message, widened his alliances and spoke directly to the voters he had lost. That is no small achievement for a politician, however experienced he may be.

But he now has to govern a country more polarised than ever. Political violence on the streets has increased, and hate speech circulates freely online.

Prominent figures on the far right, including Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, have already said they will not accept this election result. Bolsonaro said late Sunday he will not concede, and will seek an annulment of the vote.

And then there is Washington. Given the White House’s close ties to the Bolsonaro family, there is a real risk the Trump administration will question, or even refuse to recognise, the outcome of the election. That would be extraordinary, and a few years ago, it would have been unthinkable.

Things are further complicated by a legal battle on election day itself. After allegations of voter suppression of Lula’s supporters in several cities, the justices of Brazil’s Supreme Court and Supreme Electoral Court clashed over whether to extend voting hours. Whatever the legal merits, the dispute gives the losing side a ready-made narrative of “voting irregularities”.

This could be a matter of serious concern, and it may last for weeks.

Three questions for Lula’s next term

When Lula is inaugurated on January 5, three questions will define his fourth term.

The first is how Lula will govern a deeply divided country with a conservative majority in Congress and over a dozen right-wing state governors.

The legislature that held him hostage over the past four years has grown more hostile, not less. Every budget, every reform and every appointment will be a tough negotiation, with the possibility of an impeachment hanging over Lula’s head.

The second is repair. How will he deal with problems that go well beyond partisan disputes?

These include fiscal pressures from rising government spending, a steady loss of trust in democratic institutions, and an institutional system that no longer works as designed.

The Supreme Court, once the guarantor of the democratic order, has seen its legitimacy eroded by a major financial scandal surrounding Banco Master. Although the president cannot “repair” a court, he can refuse to treat the crisis as someone else’s problem.

The third question is the most important. Will Lula, his Workers’ Party (PT) and Brazil’s broader democratic forces use this reprieve to renew Brazilian politics? That would mean:

  • new political leadership alternatives beyond the ageing leaders who have dominated the left for 40 years

  • new forms of popular political participation that do not depend on a single charismatic figure

  • a new narrative that speaks to the precarious workers, religious families and angry voters who have drifted toward the far right.

This is the only real antidote to polarisation, and it will not come from a single election or a single leader.

Lula’s comeback has bought Brazil time. Whether it buys anything more depends on what he and his allies do over the next four years, one step at a time.

Lula has worked another miracle. His last task is to make sure Brazil does not need another one.

entry.title: Unlocking the secrets of the ‘Dragon Man’ skull – and what it reveals about human evolution
entry.content:
In September 2018, China Daily ran a story that found its way to my desk. It featured the photograph of a beautifully preserved fossil skull with huge brow-ridges, with a caption speculating – wrongly, as it would turn out – that it belonged to a species of human known as Homo heidelbergensis.

The article told a remarkable story about the discovery of this fossil some 85 years earlier. Japanese forces had been occupying the city of Harbin in north-eastern China in 1933. They ordered a team of local workers to help build a railway bridge across the Songhua River.

The workers uncovered the skull in river deposits, and one of them hid it from the Japanese by lowering it down a disused well. Feeling ashamed of having worked for the enemy, he kept quiet about the find for many years. Finally some 80 years later he told his son and grandson as he lay dying, which led to the almost intact skull being recovered and later donated to Hebei Geo University near Beijing.

That origin story is difficult to verify, and there were rumours that the fossil was actually a fake, but I was able to confirm first hand that it was real when I was invited to join Chinese researchers in studying this astonishing relic at the end of 2018. I jumped at this wonderful opportunity to help put one of the most complete human fossils ever found in its proper place in human evolution.

So many ways to be human

Establishing that place has got a lot trickier in the last 20 years or so. We think that humans (or hominins) split from the ancestors of our closest living relatives, the chimpanzees, about 7 million years ago. For the next 5 million years or so, the hominins continued their evolution in Africa, and about 2 million years ago, began to disperse across Asia and Europe.

It used to be thought that human evolution then progressed from more primitive forms through to modern humans (Homo sapiens), either in just one region, most likely east Africa, or across the whole inhabited world, following the early exit from Africa. Now, we know it wasn’t so simple.

Welcome to our series on the great mysteries of archaeology. Viking explorers, Amazonian cities, artefacts from before civilisation. Archaeology may be all about the past, but it’s constantly shifting with every scientific discovery. This series will dig into some of the most fascinating debates in the field today.

There was a profusion of different kinds of humans, sometimes living at the same time and even in the same regions, as nature conducted multiple experiments over millions of years in how to become human. We are the sole survivors of all those experiments.

Even during the last 300,000 years the number of human species has been startling. The ancient Homo heidelbergensis, with their heavy-set physiques and large faces and jaws, was surviving in Europe – along with similar people in Africa – 300,000 years ago. The even more ancient Homo erectus, which had a smaller brain and angular flat-topped skull, was clinging on in parts of Indonesia until at least 100,000 years ago.

Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal human), with a broad thick-set body and protruding midface around a large nose, was living in western Eurasia from at least 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. We Homo sapiens – first given that name in 1758, meaning “wise human” – existed at least 300,000 years ago, first in Africa and then globally within the last 50,000 years.

In addition, there are three enigmatic small-bodied forms (and also known to be small-brained in the first two cases) from the same recent period: Homo naledi (star human), Homo floresiensis (Flores human) and Homo luzonensis (Luzon human). These lived respectively in South Africa about 300,000 years ago; on the island of Flores, eastern Indonesia, from at least 190,000 to 50,000 years ago; and on the island of Luzon, the Philippines, about 130,000 years ago. All three seem to be long-lasting relics of even more ancient stages of human evolution.

The leading human species

Our study of the Harbin skull added yet another species to the list. When my Chinese colleagues sent me a full-size 3D print of this skull, I couldn’t believe it. I’ve seen hundreds of fossil human skulls, and this was the biggest I had ever set eyes on.

Our analyses showed it was clearly different from fossils of sapiens, neanderthalensis, heidelbergensis and erectus. It showed a distinctive combination of a very large brain size, a massive brow-ridge and a large, low but rather smooth braincase without the other bony ridges found in erectus and heidelbergensis skulls. It also had a big but modern-looking face with delicate forward-facing cheekbones but very wide nose and large eye sockets.

This warranted a new species name, and in 2021 my Chinese colleagues chose Homo longi, named after the Black Dragon River (Heilongjiang). Ever since, the skull has been known as Dragon Man. It appears that this species was in eastern Asia from at least 300,000 until about 45,000 years ago. All these human timespans are show on the chart below (click to make it bigger).

Human timespans

Enter the Denisovans

Not only did the skull turn out to be a new species of ancient human, it also helped to solve several mysteries about other discoveries. One of the keys was its single preserved tooth – a very large second molar, with no sign of a socket behind it for a third molar. In other words, Dragon Man did not have wisdom teeth.

These dental features provided a link with other less complete fossils from China that also had large molars but no wisdom teeth. This and other resemblances indicated that these were also Homo longi, overturning previous possibilities that they might have belonged to an Asian branch of Homo heidelbergensis or an interim species between Homo erectus and modern Asian humans.

It also shed light on the mysterious Denisovans, named after Denisova Cave in the Russian part of the Altai Mountains. Archaeologists had been digging there for decades, finding thousands of animal bones and stone tools, but only scraps of human bones and some large molar teeth.

In 2010 one of those bone scraps – part of a little finger – yielded ancient DNA matching the quality of modern bones. This was despite being about 60,000 years old, showing the astonishing preservation potential of this cold and dry cave in southern Siberia.

Thanks to DNA yielded from other fossils and even sediments from the site, we know the Denisovans occupied the cave intermittently from more than 200,000 until about 45,000 years ago, when Homo sapiens took over.

Placing the Denisovan genome on the human evolutionary tree was difficult, but also in 2010 a high quality Neanderthal genome was reconstructed from European fossils. The Denisovan genome was quite different both to this and to modern humans.

Fast-forward a decade and our analyses suggested that the molars found in Denisova Cave were also from the same species as the Dragon skull. More recently the Harbin skull has been analysed for DNA and fossil proteins, confirming both the connection to Denisova Cave and various other fossils found in China. These include a jawbone from a cave high up on the Tibetan plateau, bones dredged up by fishermen from off the coast of Taiwan, and remains recently described from a cave in the south-west of China.

The skull therefore turns out to be the most complete example of a species that palaeoanthropologists have been circling for some time. It’s now known by both names: Denisovan and the more formal Homo longi.

The great river of life

Having established Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes, it has been possible to compare them with those of people from around the world today. The results have been very surprising.

If people today had evolved from Neanderthals, we might have expected that modern Europeans would show the highest levels of Neanderthal DNA in their genomes, since Europe is where most Neanderthal fossils have been found over the last two centuries. It turns out they do have Neanderthal DNA, at a level of about 2%. But that level of DNA is also found throughout the world today, apart from Africa, where the level is generally much lower.

When similar comparisons were made for Denisovan DNA there were even more surprises. The highest levels were not in modern Siberians or Chinese, but in people from places like the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Australia – in some cases at levels of around 4%.

How can we explain these unexpected results? Well, we know that the vast majority of our modern human genome – more than 90% – derives from Africa. About 50,000 years ago, having evolved there, the main ancestral wave of early Homo sapiens migrated to western Asia. There they encountered local Neanderthals and did a bit of interbreeding.

That may seem impossible for different species, but today we know from thousands of genome studies that closely related species can often breed hybrids successfully. Examples include jackals and wolves, polar bears and brown bears, and Canada and Greylag geese. It can take millions of years for enough genetic differences to accumulate to make such interbreeding impossible, and that hadn’t happened in the cases of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans.

Those intermixed Homo sapiens in western Asia then spread out to every corner of the world, taking their Neanderthal DNA with them. A lot of it was selected away since it was potentially harmful, causing genetic incompatibilities in regions like the brain and reproductive organs. But other segments were kept as they helped survival, for example protecting against diseases outside of Africa. Over time, the Neanderthal DNA settled down to about the 2% of the modern genome that we see outside of Africa today.

As for the Denisovans, they too interbred with early Homo sapiens groups reaching east Asia. This happened at a lower level in mainland Asia, and seemingly at a much higher level as the Homo sapiens spread across islands of south-east Asia like Borneo and Sulawesi. So far there is no evidence that those other late-surviving relatives such as Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis contributed detectable amounts of their DNA to our genomes today. Either there was no interbreeding, or the species were too different to produce viable hybrids.

We don’t yet have fossil remains from those islands to prove the Denisovans were there before Homo sapiens, only archaeological evidence such as butchered animal bones and stone tools. But assuming this idea is correct, the Denisovans must have been a very successful and adaptable species, surviving freezing winters in northern China but also thriving in tropical grasslands in places like Sumatra. As previously mentioned, they were even living on the Tibetan plateau at altitudes above 3,000 metres.

And by the way, the same Russian cave provides evidence of another dimension to this story. DNA shows that Neanderthals were also there some of the time, and that the two species interbred. We know this from another bone fragment, whose owner, a young girl, was the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and Denisovan father.

What we got right and wrong

Most of what I’ve talked about here, we’ve only learnt in the last 16 years. For my PhD more than 50 years ago I was testing the then widespread idea that modern humans evolved directly from Neanderthals. I spent my time measuring and comparing fossil skulls, using the primitive measuring techniques and limited computing power available at the time.

I concluded that we did not evolve from them. I could see no sign that Neanderthal fossils in Europe were gradually changing towards a more modern anatomy. They weren’t developing a more rounded braincase, a smaller browridge or a more pronounced chin.

Yet now, with genetic powers that I could never have imagined, we can see that my PhD quest only gave part of the answer. Certainly we did not evolve from Neanderthals but yes, they are partly our ancestors because of that ancient interbreeding. Twenty years ago I would have told you that any interbreeding with Neanderthals was trivial in the big picture.

Together with the findings about interbreeding between modern humans and Denisovans, I have to concede that our more recent origins are only mostly out of Africa, not 100%. It means the Neanderthals and Denisovans didn’t die out completely 30,000 or 40,000 years ago: bits of their DNA live on in us today, and some of it is still active.

As for our African beginnings, it was in the 1980s and 1990s that these became clear as DNA sequences from recent human populations accumulated, as well as better fossil material. However, recent evidence suggests that our African origins were quite complex, with several lineages evolving in parallel in different parts of the continent and mixing now and again. For instance, some geneticists think ancient interbreeding with Homo heidelbergensis could have contributed to our evolution, so the human origin story keeps getting more complex.

What’s next

It’s difficult to imagine what even the next ten years will bring, as work on ancient DNA is developing so fast – along with the newer field of ancient proteomics, which studies fossil proteins. Scientists are turning to these because DNA survival is patchy, especially in warm conditions and deep time.

For example, scientists are looking for traces of the connective tissue collagen, which is widespread in our bodies, skeleton and teeth. Collagen is much more resilient than DNA, and has already been identified in fossils that are millions of years old. As the work progresses and we can sequence the different amino acids in these ancient proteins, we will start to gather knowledge of fossil relationships where DNA cannot reach, as has already been achieved for the Dragon Man fossil.

The fossil record itself will undoubtedly continue to surprise us with unexpected finds, hopefully including eagerly awaited Denisovans from the islands of south-east Asia. Also waiting to be found somewhere are fossils of first-generation hybrids between our species and the Neanderthals, and our species and the Denisovans.

Meanwhile I’m still pursuing the biggest puzzle of them all. Why are we the only surviving species out of dozens that preceded us, and the half-dozen that were still living alongside us 100,000 years ago? Did we overcome them through our better brains or better adaptations or did we just get lucky, time after time, as first the Neanderthals went under, then all the others?

I suspect competition for often limited resources was an important part of the story, where we may have been that bit more efficient than our surviving relatives, but we simply don’t know the full solution yet. More discoveries from archaeology, fossils and DNA will lead us closer to the answers.

entry.title: The Crucible: Arthur Miller’s morality tale was as much a reaction to his own marital failings as it was to the ‘red scare’
entry.content:
Written at the height of the cold war “red scare”, Arthur Miller’s 1952 play The Crucible was a retelling of the 17th-century Salem witch trials (1692-93) which soon became the classic parable of mass hysteria.

Miller’s play has long been described as “a cornerstone of American theatre” and “an allegory of our times”. Adapted into a 1996 Oscar-nominated Hollywood film, recent stage revivals on Broadway (2016) and at the UK’s National Theatre (2022) further confirm its enduring popularity.

A staple of the high-school syllabus (a YouTube search yields over 3,200 school productions), the play has also come to shape popular understandings of early modern witchcraft. As Miller (1915-2005) foresaw, its interpretation of Salem became a flexible model applicable to other tragedies – so flexible, in fact, that “witch-hunt” has in recent years devolved into a virtually meaningless political catchphrase.

While acknowledging some artistic licence, Miller still claimed to have captured Salem’s “essential nature”, insisting that “the fate of each character is exactly that of his historical model”. As a work of history, however, The Crucible is deeply flawed; as a morality tale, it can even be described as positively harmful.

Dramatic twist

The central conflict driving the play – and the witch-hunt – is sparked by the illicit romance between John Proctor, an affluent householder, and his former teenage servant, Abigail Williams. As the witch-hunt unfolds, Abigail – described in the stage instructions as “a strikingly beautiful girl … with an endless capacity for dissembling” – feigns bewitchment and accuses Proctor’s suspicious wife Elizabeth (who had dismissed her from their service) in an apparent bid to take her place.

To save his wife and undermine Abigail’s credibility, Proctor confesses the affair. This gamble, however, spectacularly backfires when Elizabeth perjures herself, denying knowledge of the relationship to save her husband’s reputation – a dramatic twist that legitimises their servant’s accusations and seals their fate.

Notoriously, the Salem court executed only those who maintained their innocence. In the final act, Proctor is offered a reprieve if he confesses to witchcraft, but he dramatically refuses to lie: “How may I live without my name? … I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” With this final defiance, the flawed hero chooses death and redeems himself. To drive that point home, the play concludes with Elizabeth’s absolution: “He have his goodness now.”

In his 1987 autobiography Timebends, Miller described visiting “half-forsaken” Salem himself and going through the records and accounts in its Historical Society building.

“Almost every testimony I had read,” he recalled, “revealed the sexual theme, either open or barely concealed.” He found “hard evidence” of Abigail Williams’s “determination to get Elizabeth murdered”, recognising in one description “the joyous terror of the killer about to strike”. In a 1996 New Yorker article, he maintained again that “John Proctor had bedded Abigail”.

John Proctor was indeed one of the 19 victims of the Salem witch-hunt; Elizabeth survived the panic, her execution at first postponed because of a pregnancy. The real-life Proctor had also been a scathing critic of the court’s use of spectral evidence – the diabolical fits supposedly experienced by the child accusers.

This, however, is where the historical evidence and Miller’s drama diverge. Proctor was in his sixties, not in “his middle thirties”. Abigail Williams is presented as 17 in the play; she is played by a 24-year-old Winona Ryder on screen. Miller acknowledged that “Abigail’s age had been raised” but never stated by how much. Contemporary sources make clear that she was at most 12 years old. There is no evidence she was ever Proctor’s servant, let alone his lover.

Art imitating life

All too often, when we study early modern witches, we see ourselves. Miller’s supposed “hard evidence” was little more than personal projection. In Timebends, the playwright admitted that he “had been searching a long time for a tragic hero”. In the New Yorker, he reflected how his own marital failings had caused him to empathise with Proctor:

My own marriage of 12 years was teetering and I knew more than I wished to know about where the blame lay. That John Proctor the sinner might overturn his paralysing personal guilt and become the most forthright voice against the madness around him was a reassurance to me, and, I suppose, an inspiration.

This relatable Proctor did not exist; Miller had invented him.

This points to two ways in which The Crucible is a deeply problematic work of fiction. First, by blaming the Salem tragedy on Abigail Williams, Miller roots a witch-hunt – of all things – in female malice. Second, by constructing Proctor as his hero, the playwright also employs the play and its supposed historic content as a vehicle for his own redemption.

Underpinning both distortions is a refusal to engage with the complexities of history. They show how easy and tempting it is to simply invert the original moral polarity, transforming not only accused witches into saints, but an allegedly bewitched child into a conniving teenage vixen.

Historians now recognise that many of Salem’s young accusers were deeply traumatised survivors of the Indian Wars (1688–1697); some even witnessed the brutal murder of their parents. Abigail, too, was orphaned, though the cause remains unknown.

Attributing blame and responsibility is rarely as straightforward as we would like it to be. Historical research requires careful study of both the evidence and our own biases.

The Crucible does not capture the “essential nature” of the Salem witch-hunt, but it does reveal a great deal about its mid-20th century author – and the anxieties, desires and misogyny that drove him.

entry.title: How Lula turned four lessons from the presidential elections in Colombia into a comeback in Brazil’s Sunday runoff
entry.content:
On the night of last 4 October, Brazil’s left woke up to the scenario it had discredited for months. Far right senator Flávio Bolsonaro finished the first round in the country’s presidential election roughly two million votes ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (47% to 45% of the valid votes). The polls that had shown the incumbent president comfortably ahead for most of the year had misled both his campaign and its supporters, and the Bolsonaro campaign moved quickly to turn surprise into destiny. Within days, Flávio was speaking about who would be his ministers and policy priorities as if the runoff were a mere formality.

The script was, in many ways, borrowed from Colombia. On 21 June, Abelardo de la Espriella won that country’s presidency by roughly 250,000 votes out of more than 25 million cast — 49.7 percent against Iván Cepeda’s 48.7 — in one of the highest-turnout elections in its history. The right has since sold that result as the opening act of a renewed regional tide that Brazil was bound to follow.

The narrative of inevitability was always wrong, but the Colombian diagnosis was not. Cepeda’s defeat isolated four variables the Latin American left has consistently mismanaged. What is striking about the last three weeks is that Lula’s campaign, after stumbling into them, appears to have learned the lessons. Three days before the vote, the race is a dead heat, and the momentum is on the president’s side.

Reframing the incumbency curse

The first lesson concerns the arithmetic of contemporary incumbency. Cepeda lost while gaining the largest absolute vote the Colombian left has ever obtained. His defeat was not a collapse of the progressive coalition but the discovery of its ceiling, set by the outgoing Gustavo Petro administration.

No sitting president in South America enjoys majority support today. Low economic growth, fiscal constraint and the routinization of anti-establishment sentiment have made governing itself electorally costly. Lula, whose approval has trailed his disapproval for much of his third term, is no exception. The first round showed that a lead built on a fragmented, scandal-weakened opposition is not the same thing as governmental popularity, and that it evaporates once a challenger consolidates.

The campaign’s answer has been to stop running a referendum and start running a choice. Instead of focusing on the legacy of his earlier governments, Lula is now trying to showcase his unparalleled experience, setting it against a challenger with no executive record of his own. The effect is visible in the one number incumbents most need to move: in a survey released on 21 October, the share of voters who say they would never vote for Lula fell from 53% to 47% percent in a single week, while Flávio’s rejection eased only from 54% to 52%.

From overconfidence to shock therapy

The second lesson is about complacency and its distributive roots. Cepeda’s Pacto Histórico party entered Colombia’s first round convinced it could win outright. A conviction that licensed minimal media exposure, refusal to debate, and mobilization rather than persuasion. Lula’s first round looked uncomfortably similar: a candidate coasting on favourable polls, investing little in reaching beyond a base that proved insufficient.

The difference is what happened next. In less than a week, the campaign reinvented itself, both on social media and on the streets. A combination of aggressive digital content and grassroots mobilization, from neighborhood canvassing to large rallies in states where the left had gone quiet, changed the mood of the runoff. A campaign that had been talking to the converted started looking for the persuadable – a mass of 33 million voters who did not show up for the first round.

More importantly, it began speaking to the constituency Cepeda lost. Poverty reduction remains the left’s strongest policy claim and its weakest electoral instrument, because its beneficiaries are already committed and its non-beneficiaries increasingly see themselves as its funders. Brazil’s version of that problem is an urban periphery whose aspirations are organized around work, credit and informal entrepreneurship rather than redistribution. In the middle of the runoff, Lula secured Senate approval for ending the six-day work week and renegotiated the debts of small businesses and self-employed workers. These measures speak to exactly the lower-middle-class voters who decided Colombia, and they allow Lula to talk about the future with something already delivered.

Contesting the right’s ownership of the security agenda

Third, public security has displaced the economy as the organizing issue of Latin American electorates, and the right has captured it almost without a fight. De la Espriella campaigned against the negotiated demobilization of armed groups, while Cepeda, personally identified with Petro’s Paz Total (Total Peace) strategy, spent the runoff qualifying a policy that had become indefensible. His concession came across as opportunism rather than learning.

Brazil’s federal structure makes the terrain even harder for Lula: security is constitutionally a matter for the local states, which lets opposition governors claim credit for successful operations while blaming the federal government for any failures.

The left’s standard reply — that crime is downstream of poverty and inequality — is defensible in theory and weak at the ballot box. Lula’s campaign has chosen a different route. Rather than retreating, it has turned the question of organized crime toward his opponent, intensifying attacks on Flávio’s record, from corruption allegations to alleged ties to criminal groups in Rio de Janeiro.

The decisive moment came in last Sunday’s TV debate, when Lula challenged both candidates to disclose their bank statements. It was a simple but powerful gesture that converted an abstract integrity argument into a test Flávio had to answer on camera. Surely, Lula’s campaign has not yet matched the right’s Mano Dura with an institutional security agenda of its own, and that remains a gap for a possible fourth term. But it has stopped conceding the issue.

Foreign leaders as an internal variable

Fourth, De la Espriella borrowed heavily from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, from his security strategy to his public image. For a substantial middle-class electorate, the images of the CECOT megaprison offered a practical-looking blueprint, and 53.8 percent of Colombians held a favorable view of the Salvadoran president.

Brazil differs in degree and, arguably, in kind, because its longstanding tensions with the United States sit at the center of the story. Sovereignty runs deep in Brazilian political culture, and Lula drew real advantage from confronting Washington’s tariff pressure in 2025.

But the rally-around-the-flag effect has diminishing returns: a tariff is felt in employment before it is felt in dignity, and earlier surveys found fewer than half of voters accepting Lula’s claim that these measures were the product of his opponent’s lobbying. The runoff campaign appears to have understood this, shifting its weight from sovereignty rhetoric toward kitchen-table delivery and leaving foreign policy as background rather than headline.

What the comparison now tells us

Colombia’s runoff was decided by one percentage point. Brazil’s will likely be just as close. Datafolha’s 15 October survey had Flávio at 51% of valid votes against Lula’s 49%, down from 52% to 48% a week earlier. Quaest’s survey released on 21 October puts the race at Flávio 45% to Lula 44% in total voting intentions, inside the margin of error, with the two candidates tied at 40% percent when voters are asked without being shown names. Every trend line in these numbers runs toward the president.

Colombia was never evidence of an ideological tide. It was a narrow and specific failure: the inability to speak to voters who are neither poor enough to be beneficiaries nor wealthy enough to be adversaries, compounded by a campaign that realized too late that it was losing. Brazil’s left got its warning on 4 October, with three weeks still on the clock. The good news for the Workers’ Party is that it seems to have listened. Whether that is enough will be decided on Sunday.

entry.title: How K-dramas use Africa as a backdrop to boost South Korea’s image
entry.content:
The success of South Korean popular music or K-pop continues to power the Hallyu Wave, a term that describes the global obsession with the country’s pop culture production.

But before K-pop came the spread of K-drama, TV series from the country, starting in the late 1990s. By 2024 the melodrama Queen of Tears ranked as the most watched Korean series on Netflix, becoming the 14th most watched show of all time on the streaming service. It followed on the success of many other hits like Crash Landing on You and Marry My Husband.

K-drama has led to the development of another trend: Africa repeatedly appears as a homogeneous place full of savage danger or childish immaturity, and in need of a Korean saviour.

As a scholar of film and media, with a specific interest in global Black art and film practices, I recently studied how and why Africa became this trope in K-drama. This is particularly true in rags-to-riches romance stories and melodramas.

I traced Africa’s presence in three K-dramas – Shooting Stars (2022), Marry My Husband (2024) and Queen of Tears (2024). In them, Africa appears in three different negative ways:

  • in need of charity

  • a place of rebellion and savagery

  • a place of punishment for a “troubled” child.

My intention wasn’t to say why these portrayals are bad, but rather to understand what they reveal about South Korea. How they function as a scale for measuring and emphasising South Korea’s own development.

No longer the poor post-war country of the late 1950s, South Korea can now position itself among leading world powers. It has grown in the global economic and cultural landscapes.

Yet, as I argue in my study, what allows countries like this to define their developmental status is their ability to distinguish themselves from Africa. I propose that Africa’s presence in K-dramas is as a place maker, or specifically image-maker. Africa’s “savage” presence serves as a way of distinguishing the emerging soft power of South Korea, where what benefits the country’s global image is the ability to provide aid to Africa.

A place to do good

In his book On the Postcolony, Cameroonian philosopher Achille Mbembe describes Africa as Europe’s “signifier”. This means that the way Europe comes to know and define itself is only possible through how it defines itself against Africa.

But my study contributes to showing that this is not just the case in the west. The ever-growing presence of eastern soft powers such as China and South Korea means that longstanding stereotypes of Africa have found new sites of replenishment.

There are some major threads that connected Africa’s presence in the K-dramas I studied. One is its portrayal as a place where non-Africans could go to build character by participating in volunteer work as part of an NGO. In Marry my Husband, for example, the show’s antagonist Oh Yu-ra loses her job in the family business and is sent to “join a volunteer foundation in Africa to build character”.

In Shooting Stars, this idea of Africa as the epicentre of charity is even more apparent. The show’s opening sequence features the main character digging wells in Africa. He’s accompanied by smiling village children and a sound that one viewer described as “Lion King music”.

In both shows, South Korea is personified through the characters sent to Africa. While Yu-ra is sent as punishment, the character in Shooting Stars is an actor whose volunteer trip aids in his public image in South Korea. Africa becomes what builds the image and character of others, but only by being relegated to a cliché.

Yu-ra’s punishment shows how Africa becomes the K-drama’s vessel to hold the unwanted or defamed of other nations. It collects what disrupts the happiness of romance and, by extension, of nation-making, in South Korea. This figuration of the continent reappears in Queen of Tears.

A lawless continent

Queen of Tears does not follow the Asian-saviour-in-Africa trope. Instead, it presents Africa as a place for youthful inhibitions, with no sense of order or rule of law. The ideal place for the kinds of behaviours that might be illegal in the more “civilized” South Korean society that the character exists in.

In Africa’s brief cameo in the show’s third episode, the younger brother of the show’s protagonist, Soo-Cheol, reminisces on his rebellious days:

I’m reminded of when I went to Africa. My twenties were filled with wildness and barbarism.

When chided that he stayed in his hotel for most of the trip, Soo-Cheol comments, “I had enough of the wildness just looking out of the window.”

Here, Africa is understood in proximity to danger and savagery. Is it that there are no crime, criminals, or places and people in need of saving in South Korea? The obvious answer is no, but as my study finds, when viewed through these shows, the answer reads more like, “Compared to Africa, yes.”

Where will Africa go next?

This treatment of Africa began long before the shows in my study. Africa’s character-building qualities appear, for example, in the 2018 film Burning. The film’s female protagonist goes on a “soul-searching” quest to find life’s greater meaning.

In unscripted variety shows, African immigrants living in South Korea, like Sam Okyere or Jonathan Yiombi, often feature as hosts or guests, but not without their share of racist backlash.

Okyere, for example, was subject to racist comments after criticising a video of South Korean students recreating a popular video from his home country, Ghana. The same happened to Yiombi after South Korea was eliminated from the football World Cup because the DRC, his country of birth, defeated Uzbekistan, indirectly causing South Korea to be eliminated.

For better or worse, Africa’s metaphorical and literal presence has come to occupy South Korea’s cultural and aesthetic imagination. Despite Africa also being a continent full of modern urban life, cultural riches and innovation, the clichés remain.

Read more: Streaming giants have helped bring Korean dramas to the world – but much is lost in translation

This presence is only possible through the expected and invented image of the savage, helpless and primitive, who is in need, even after independence, of more civilising. And not only from western colonial powers, but also from the growing economies of the east.

A symbol of lack

K-dramas are increasingly popular in Africa, yet when constantly viewed this way, Hallyu’s success in Africa comes with a heavy representational price.

Despite their engagement with K-drama, African audiences can only ever seem to see themselves represented through a colonial gaze that benefits South Korea’s pursuit of global power. Africa then, while continuing to build South Korea’s cultural capital, can only ever exist as a symbol of lack.

entry.title: America’s death penalty: why executions are rising again
entry.content:
After two decades of decline, the number of executions in the United States began rising sharply again in 2025. Last year, 47 people were put to death – the highest number in more than 15 years. So far in 2026, another 31 people have been executed.

The resurgence comes amid renewed controversy over capital punishment, following the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee and a proposal to livestream a military execution, which President Donald Trump subsequently walked back.

But according to Carolyn Strange, emeritus professor of history at the Australian National University, these controversies have striking precedents in American history.

Pike is not the first person to survive an execution attempt. In 1946, Willie Francis survived the electric chair in Louisiana. After an unsuccessful legal challenge, the state executed him in 1947.

Strange says the history of capital punishment in the US is marked by repeated attempts to make executions more humane – or at least appear that way. From the electric chair to lethal injections, new methods were introduced with the promise of making death quicker and more efficient.

Lethal injection, for example, has the appearance of an ordinary medical procedure. “It seems normal, it seems clean, it seems clinical, civilised,” Strange says.

Yet Pike’s case raises questions about whether the method has lived up to that promise.

Strange also argues it’s misleading to talk about a single American approach to the death penalty.

It’s really better to talk about the death penalty in the disunited states.

While some states abolished capital punishment more than a century ago, others continue to embrace it. Florida, under governor Ron DeSantis, has been responsible for a substantial share of the recent rise in executions. In 2025, Florida carried out 19 executions – 40% of the year’s total.

And while support in the US for the death penalty has declined over recent decades, the issue remains deeply divisive. For Strange, the history of capital punishment reveals something fundamental about American politics:

The most important thing is that capital punishment and the death penalty is about politics, not justice.

entry.title: Hokusai’s Great Wave is one of 46 prints of Mount Fuji – seeing them together changes everything
entry.content:
When I first saw Katsushika Hokusai’s Clear Day with a Southern Breeze (also known as Red Fuji, 1830-1833), I was struck by its lustrous red resonating against the receding blue of the sky. Clouds align gently in an almost humorous formation. Near the peak of the mountain, are creases of snow. At its foot we are drawn to a multitude of tiny trees amassed in chorus. Easy to overlook, they change the picture. The great mountain becomes itself in relation to everything that surrounds it.

Dulwich Picture Gallery is showing all of Hokusai’s 36 Views of Mount Fuji, including ten added after the series became popular. Hokusai made them in his seventies in the early 1830s as cheap prints for ordinary people in Edo (today’s Tokyo). It is the first, and perhaps only, time the complete series will be shown together in the UK.

One image is instantly recognisable: The Great Wave (actually titled Under the Wave off Kanagawa). Seen alongside the others, it becomes one view among many – and a lesson in how quickly we settle on a single view of anything, including each other.

Three versions of Mount Fuji hang together in the first room. In Red Fuji the mountain is almost pure form. A light blue variant, its ridge edged in heavy indigo, opens a way into the mountain. A third, with lightning like cracks in a pot, feels dark and unsettled.

On the opposite wall hangs The Great Wave. Its foam reaches out like grasping, knuckled fingers, and flecks scatter across the dark water like stars in the night. Everything should be in motion, yet the print holds a stillness. Beneath the wave is Fuji again: a tiny triangle here where Red Fuji’s was expansive. It is the same mountain, but now framed by the sea.

Elsewhere, people hurry over bridges, work in fields and travel along roads. Hills seem to wear patterned bandanas of farmland, while Prussian blue skies fade at a soft, feathered edge. Shapes mingle playfully: three haystacks echo the three small peaks of Fuji’s summit. Hokusai places us in between, looking down on people and up at the sky, but never from a position that reveals everything.

In the third room, one print stopped me. In Mishima Pass in Kai Province, travellers link arms around an enormous tree. I saw an affectionate embrace, then learned they may be measuring its girth. How quickly I had decided what these strangers felt.

As an art psychotherapist, I work with exactly this. We imagine what others might be thinking and feeling, drawing on our own experience – therapists call this mentalising, and doing it well means staying with curiosity rather than assuming we know. I have never been to Japan and cannot experience Fuji as Hokusai’s first viewers did. What reaches me is what colour, form and shape do, across that distance.

Hokusai’s giant tree also recalls an experiment on awe in which people who had gazed up at towering eucalyptus trees for a minute picked up more of a researcher’s “accidentally” dropped pens than those who had looked at a building. A print may not make us kinder, but when we do feel part of a bigger picture, we may just become a bit less absorbed in ourselves, and perhaps more open to others.

The curation is less subtle than the prints. Its dusky blue walls echo Hokusai’s colours, but I was left cold. I felt fixed as a viewer, each picture held apart when I wanted to see how they connect – although the soft lighting creates an atmosphere, a quietness that simply lets you be with them.

At the end of the series, pilgrims climb into Fuji itself. Each looks much like the next, like frames of a stop-motion film. Near the summit they crowd into a shelter in the rock, a small window into something none could enter alone. We no longer look towards a distant mountain; we are drawn into it, among people making their own way upwards.

I left thinking about The Great Wave very differently. I could see the little mountain beneath it, but also the trees, travellers and pilgrims. The Fuji I began with had amassed a sense of journey, unfolding across the series.

Hokusai: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from the Iuchi Collection is on at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London until January 17, 2027

entry.summary: The prints create a story that expands our understanding of the now famous Great Wave.

entry.title: Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why
entry.content:
More than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out.

Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health.

People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras.

Napoleon and gymnastics

In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry.

As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French.

The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825.

The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century.

The birth of bodybuilding

A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest.

But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted.

From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa.

Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training.

Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic.

Read more: Fitness gurus and ‘muscular Christianity’: how Victorian Britain anticipated today’s keep fit craze

Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake.

The post-war aerobics boom

The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity.

In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom.

New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing.

The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room.

The muscle builders

In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it.

Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible.

Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies.

Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics.

By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok.

Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema.

Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm.
